title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis
authors: Yongcun Song, Shangzhi Zeng, Jin Zhang, Lvgang Zhang
abstract: Mesh-free partial differential equation (PDE) solvers construct discrete systems from residuals at sampled points. These solvers fit coefficients in a parameterized trial representation and select solver-design parameters governing the representation, training-residual weighting, and regularization. These parameters strongly affect solution accuracy, yet existing selection strategies are largely tailored to particular solver classes. To address this limitation, we formulate a unified validation-driven bilevel optimization framework applicable across different solver classes, in which the lower level fits coefficients using training collocation residuals, while the upper level selects solver-design parameters using held-out validation residuals. For nonlinear PDEs, however, solving the nonlinear lower-level problem to high accuracy is costly, while the adjoint system is typically ill-conditioned and indefinite. To address this issue, we propose an efficient implicit hypergradient method that approximates the lower-level response using finite, warm-started damped Gauss-Newton (GN) updates. For the adjoint solve, we use the damped GN matrix to compute an initial adjoint and to precondition a finite number of minimum residual iterations. To quantify the errors introduced by these approximations, we derive local hypergradient error bounds that separate the contributions of the finite lower-level solve, adjoint damping, and the final adjoint residual. Combining this analysis with validation sampling bounds and residual stability, we relate validation residuals to PDE solution accuracy and establish error bounds for the computed PDE solution. Numerical experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed method across Kansa, random feature and extreme learning machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers.

infographic.key_insight: Validation-driven bilevel optimization tunes mesh-free PDE solver designs, while error analysis connects approximate hypergradients and validation residuals to solution accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides a unified way to tune representation, residual weighting, and regularization across multiple mesh-free solver classes.
method: Fit trial coefficients on training collocation residuals; tune solver-design parameters on held-out validation residuals.
Approximate nonlinear lower-level solutions with finite, warm-started damped Gauss–Newton updates.
Use the damped Gauss–Newton matrix to initialize and precondition adjoint iterations, with bounds separating key approximation errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on several nonlinear PDEs, including a high-dimensional problem, report accuracy and efficiency across Kansa, random-feature/extreme-learning-machine, and physics-informed neural network solvers; the abstract gives no numerical metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Hypergradient bounds are local, and translating validation residuals into solution-error guarantees depends on sampling bounds and residual stability.
infographic.paper_title: A Validation-Driven Bilevel Optimization Method for Mesh-Free PDE Solvers and Its Error Analysis

title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
authors: Jiashu Li, Tianyu Gao, Qinglong Liu, Jinping Wang, Ye Wei, Zhiqiang Gao
abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Atomic MathReasoner improves mathematical LLMs by selecting a problem-specific composition of specialized reasoning skills rather than treating reasoning as one monolithic capability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A lightweight router selects among precomputed LoRA expert compositions, enabling adaptive specialization without costly online optimization.
method: Train capability-specific LoRA experts and discover low-loss composition prototypes through gradient-free optimization on held-out validation subsets.
Score prototypes using reference-solution token-level negative log-likelihood and filter ambiguous assignments with a confidence margin.
Distill the resulting pseudo-labels into a router that selects a composition prototype for each input problem.
infographic.evidence_signal: On AtomicMath with Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR raises average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, and average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond AtomicMath remains unestablished in the abstract, and deployment requires offline expert training, prototype optimization, and router supervision.
infographic.paper_title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs

title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning
authors: Umberto Biccari, Junqing Huang, Kang Liu, Enrique Zuazua
abstract: Generative models transform simple random inputs into samples that resemble observed data. For a finite training set, a central question is how its geometry shapes the terminal dynamics and the probabilities assigned to individual samples. We address this question for flow matching with linear interpolation between independent Gaussian and empirical samples. The squared distance to the training set generates explicit paths contracting exponentially toward the nearest sample. We prove that exact trajectories restarted at prescribed late-time states approximate these paths uniformly over all elapsed times and compact sets of starting states away from Voronoi interfaces, with an error exponentially small in the inverse squared restart noise scale. The initial mass near interfaces controls the quadratic Wasserstein error between the exact and reference laws. For Gaussian and fixed Gaussian-tube restart laws, this gives a square-root rate in the restart noise scale, uniform over time, which a two-site example shows to be sharp in general. At ties, the Clarke subdifferential characterizes the graphical limit of the rescaled velocity field. This geometry motivates two learning methods: fitting the distance potential with value and gradient supervision, and fitting velocities along explicit contraction paths. A transport estimate separates initialization mismatch, velocity error, incomplete contraction, and endpoint allocation. MNIST experiments illustrate the distinct roles of support proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity. These results connect flow matching and score-based diffusion through a common limiting geometry and show how asymptotic analysis can inform the design and evaluation of generative models.

infographic.key_insight: Near terminal time, flow matching follows the training set’s distance geometry, with trajectories approximating exponential contraction toward the nearest sample away from Voronoi boundaries.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This geometry motivates distance-potential and path-based velocity learning, while separating initialization, velocity, contraction, and sample-allocation errors.
method: Analyze Gaussian-to-empirical flow matching using explicit nearest-sample contraction paths.
Bound trajectory and distribution errors, with Clarke subdifferentials describing limiting velocities at ties.
Learn either a distance potential with value-and-gradient supervision or velocities along contraction paths.
infographic.evidence_signal: A two-site example establishes sharpness of the general square-root Wasserstein rate, while MNIST experiments distinguish support proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity.
infographic.watch_item: Uniform trajectory guarantees exclude Voronoi interfaces, and proximity to training samples alone does not establish correct sample allocation or feature fidelity.
infographic.paper_title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning

title: The Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology: A Methodological Shift from the Perspective of Natural Science and Engineering Practice
authors: Shengchang Chen
abstract: Mainstream artificial intelligence systems, fundamentally driven by the Optimization-Driven (OD) paradigm, rely on setting external objectives and iterative trial-and-error. When confronted with complex nonlinear problems containing noise and conflicting constraints, this paradigm inherently induces statistical smoothing and compromise, yielding black-box models that lack interpretability and out-of-distribution generalization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes the Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology, reconstructing the solving process into four irreversible stages: Deconstruction, Structure, Construction, and Solving. The method suspends a priori presuppositions to strip unit coupling, extracts rigid invariants inherent to the problem, constructs equivalent mappings anchored to these invariants, and executes the mapping directly to generate the solution. Evaluation metrics and experience are relegated to a posteriori verification. Demonstrated through cross-disciplinary practices including number theory, Hamiltonian systems, deep learning, and seismic inversion, this methodology transcends the statistical fitting bottleneck. Structure-Driven and Objective-Driven methodologies are complementary: when structure is sufficient, solutions are directly constructed; when lacking, it degenerates into the OD path.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes replacing objective-driven trial-and-error with a structure-driven process that constructs solutions from a problem’s inherent invariants.
infographic.engineering_relevance: When sufficient structure is identifiable, invariant-based mappings could reduce reliance on iterative fitting and make engineering solutions more interpretable.
method: Deconstruct the problem by suspending prior assumptions and separating coupled units.
Extract rigid invariants and construct equivalent mappings anchored to them.
Execute the mappings to obtain solutions, using metrics and experience for posterior verification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract cites demonstrations in number theory, Hamiltonian systems, deep learning, and seismic inversion, but reports no datasets, quantitative results, or benchmark comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Practical success depends on identifying sufficient invariants and valid mappings; the approach falls back to objective-driven methods when structure is insufficient.
infographic.paper_title: The Four-Element Theory of Structure-Driven Methodology: A Methodological Shift from the Perspective of Natural Science and Engineering Practice

title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research
authors: Hai Wang, Bretislav Hajek, Chonghe Jiang, Minwei Kong, Ao Qu, Huatian Gong
abstract: Operations research (OR) relies on algorithms that experts tailor to each problem: a new routing, scheduling or network design problem can take weeks of specialist work before it is solved well at scale. Large language model (LLM) agents now write, test and improve code, but whether they can design algorithms that scale to realistic instances is open: in the FrontierOR benchmark's one-shot evaluation, the strongest model matches Gurobi, with an objective within 1% of Gurobi's and no slower, on only 39% of the large instances. The FrontierOR Challenge asks teams to build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve algorithms for many optimization problems at once. Stage 1 releases 60 of the benchmark's 180 audited problems, spanning six application categories and five formulation types, in weekly rounds of 15; Stage 2 introduces new problems outside the benchmark, with unseen instances. Two tracks are ranked separately: in the Main track we run the submitted algorithms in a network-isolated sandbox with open-source dependencies only; in the Self-hosted track teams solve the instances on their own machines, with any software, within a timed window. Every solution is checked for feasibility, and a feasible solution scores the ratio of its objective to a frozen known reference, averaged over hidden instances.

infographic.key_insight: The FrontierOR Challenge tests whether LLM-agent workflows can design scalable optimization algorithms across diverse operations research problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Automated algorithm design could reduce specialist effort for routing, scheduling, and network design, but reliable performance at realistic scale remains unproven.
method: Build agentic workflows that design, test, and improve optimization algorithms.
Stage 1 releases 60 audited problems; Stage 2 adds new problems with unseen instances.
Evaluate separately in a network-isolated Main track and a timed Self-hosted track.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the benchmark’s one-shot evaluation, the strongest model achieved an objective within 1% of Gurobi’s with no slower runtime on only 39% of large instances; challenge scoring checks feasibility and averages objective-to-reference ratios over hidden instances.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports a baseline and challenge protocol, not demonstrated gains from submitted agentic workflows.
infographic.paper_title: The FrontierOR Challenge: Agentic Algorithm Design for Operations Research

title: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers
authors: Michael G. Medvedev, Nikolai V. Krivoshchapov, Stepan N. Ostarkov
abstract: Language models are now used throughout all sciences - for reading literature, extracting numbers from tables and spectra, analyzing data, drafting conclusions - and their answers arrive in the same polished confident tone whether they are right or wrong, so a result has to be re-derived by a human researcher before it can be relied on. The cost of that re-checking, not the ability to generate results, is what currently limits AI-assisted research. In the field of mathematics, this problem is solved by proof assistants like Lean 4 and Coq that let any formal statement and its proof be written down and checked - a perfect match for LLMs, which are now actively used to search for proofs with every step automatically validated, rather than relying on a human to judge the result. In this paper, we propose an extension of this approach to non-mathematical sciences. We describe an AI agent harness that aims to make LLM's scientific reasoning verifiable: the starting assumptions are proposed by LLM and reviewed by a human, and everything built on top of them is checked by a machine with Lean 4. We illustrate how this mechanism works in practice on several examples and our results show that scientific arguments in these tasks can be expressed as formal proofs from explicit assumptions, including experimental results, known theoretical statements, and additional assumptions, produced by the agent. We suggest that this approach could change how scientific research is conducted across all sciences.

infographic.key_insight: Scientific arguments generated by LLMs can be formalized and machine-checked, while human researchers remain responsible for reviewing their starting assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A Lean 4 verification layer could reduce manual checking of AI-generated scientific reasoning by separating explicit assumptions from formally validated deductions.
method: An LLM agent proposes starting assumptions for human review.
The agent formalizes scientific arguments using experimental results, theoretical statements, and additional assumptions.
Lean 4 checks deductions against the stated assumptions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports several examples demonstrating formal proofs of scientific arguments, but provides no quantitative evaluation or benchmark details.
infographic.watch_item: Formal verification establishes correctness relative to assumptions, not the empirical truth of those assumptions or their adequacy for modeling reality.
infographic.paper_title: Self-verifiable LLM-driven science and why it needs human researchers

title: AI-Assisted Decision Support for Formula 1 Pit-Stop Strategy: Deep Reinforcement Learning and Mathematical Programming
authors: Felipe Méndez, Charles Thraves
abstract: Pit-stop strategy in Formula 1 is a sequential decision problem under uncertainty, in which strategists decide at each lap whether to pit and which tire compound to fit. We develop a data-driven simulator, calibrated with historical race data, that captures tire degradation, drivers' recent performance, overtaking, yellow flag events, and rivals' pit-stop decisions. We train agents with five Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) algorithms and compare them with a Quadratic Mixed-Integer Programming (QMIP) formulation that is optimal in deterministic single-driver settings. Without uncertainty or competition, all DRL methods except TRPO achieve near-optimal performance. With a full grid of competitors and stochastic race events, the ranking of DRL methods depends on the evaluation setting: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and its recurrent variant are the only methods that improve on the QMIP both in fully simulated races and when the actual 2024 races are replayed. Averaged over eight circuits, PPO improves on the QMIP by 0.33 and 0.49 positions in the two settings and Recurrent PPO by less, and in the replay PPO finishes 0.66 positions ahead of the drivers' actual strategies simulated in the same races. The QMIP performs similarly to the other methods, even though it cannot anticipate yellow flag events. Finally, we use the trained PPO policy as a look-ahead decision-support tool that shows the strategist the distribution of race outcomes under each candidate pit-stop action. Applied retrospectively to eight 2024 races, the look-ahead identifies the laps where the actual decision, the recommendation, or a third action was preferable.

infographic.key_insight: PPO-based pit-stop planning modestly outperformed mathematical optimization under race uncertainty and enabled action-by-action forecasts of finishing outcomes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining reinforcement learning with a calibrated simulator can support sequential operational decisions where uncertainty and competitors limit deterministic optimization.
method: Calibrate a race simulator with historical data, including tire wear, overtaking, yellow flags, and rival pit stops.
Compare five deep reinforcement learning algorithms against a quadratic mixed-integer programming baseline.
Use trained PPO for look-ahead comparisons of outcome distributions under candidate pit-stop actions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight circuits, PPO averaged 0.33 positions better than QMIP in simulated races and 0.49 in 2024 race replays; in replays, it also beat simulated actual driver strategies by 0.66 positions.
infographic.watch_item: Results are simulation-based and retrospective; real-time deployment would require validation of simulator fidelity and robustness to unseen race conditions.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Decision Support for Formula 1 Pit-Stop Strategy: Deep Reinforcement Learning and Mathematical Programming

title: PWLNet: A Framework for Linearized Neural Surrogates in Nonlinear Process Optimization
authors: Sunoy Sanyal, Canberk Demir, Metin Türkay, Erdal Aydın
abstract: Neural networks represent nonlinear process systems accurately, but embedding them in optimization is difficult because smooth activations introduce nonlinear, nonconvex constraints. PWLNet is a Python framework for building optimization-compatible neural surrogates through exact and piecewise-linear reformulations. It combines baseline and physics-informed training, optimization-aware pruning, and Pyomo embeddings based on ReLU mixed-integer linear models, exact tanh nonlinear models, PWL-tanh formulations, and binary-free SOSX branch-and-LP. PWL-native training uses the same activation in training and embedding, avoiding extra linearization error. It is evaluated on Boston housing, the Williams-Otto process, the Van de Vusse reactor, and a hydroformylation semi-batch reactor. On Boston housing, SOSX training gave the best common-architecture model (test MAE 1.984, R2 = 0.925). On Williams-Otto, pruning 15% of hidden neurons reduced MILP solution time 6.5-fold while preserving the selected operating point. For the Van de Vusse reactor, a physics-informed ReLU RNN pruned from 32 to 12 hidden units enabled tractable exact MILP embedding and a 4% true-plant economic gain over the best ramp-and-hold policy, while terminal-aware shrinking-horizon prediction reached 99.7% of the direct-shooting reference. For the hydroformylation reactor, one-step exact-tanh IPOPT reached 99.2% of the certified reference product with peak pressure 20.002 bar (limit 20 bar) and 14.36 s total solve time over 280 moves; ReLU and PWL-native controllers achieved comparable recovery, with ReLU fastest. Longer horizons and physics-informed training did not consistently improve closed-loop results. Overall, compact linearized neural surrogates enable accurate, tractable optimization in steady-state and dynamic applications, with constraint fidelity identified as a key direction for improvement.

infographic.key_insight: PWLNet makes neural process surrogates optimization-compatible through exact or piecewise-linear reformulations, with compact models enabling tractable optimization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can embed learned steady-state and dynamic process models in Pyomo to optimize operating conditions and control policies.
method: Train baseline or physics-informed networks and prune hidden neurons for optimization efficiency.
Embed ReLU, exact-tanh, or PWL-tanh models using MILP, nonlinear, or binary-free SOSX formulations.
Use PWL-native training to match training and embedding activations, avoiding added linearization error.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four benchmarks, reported results include 6.5× faster Williams–Otto MILP solves after 15% pruning and a 4% true-plant economic gain over the best ramp-and-hold policy for Van de Vusse.
infographic.watch_item: Constraint fidelity remains a concern: hydroformylation exact-tanh control reached 20.002 bar against a 20-bar limit, and longer horizons or physics-informed training did not consistently improve closed-loop results.
infographic.paper_title: PWLNet: A Framework for Linearized Neural Surrogates in Nonlinear Process Optimization

title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework
authors: Bjørn André Aaslund, Johannes Berge, Ayoub Haida, Ying Ni, Rita Pimentel
abstract: We propose X Hedging, an alternative to the Deep Hedging framework that addresses computational and explainability limitations of neural-network-based hedging strategies. Deep Hedging leverages neural networks to learn flexible hedging policies but relies on opaque models and typically requires large training datasets, which can complicate interpretation and limit its effectiveness in data-constrained settings. X Hedging takes a step toward addressing these limitations by replacing neural networks with tree ensemble methods, specifically LightGBM, to estimate hedging strategies. This design provides a computationally efficient alternative while preserving strong hedging performance and moving toward more user-centered explainability. To integrate LightGBM into a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework, we introduce an optimization approach that sequentially trains tree-ensemble models while introducing stochasticity through random training orders. In controlled experiments, X Hedging achieves performance comparable to Deep Hedging while offering greater user-centered explainability, improved computational efficiency, and substantially higher robustness when training data are limited. The numerical results demonstrate that tree-ensemble methods provide an effective computational alternative to neural networks for data-driven dynamic hedging.

infographic.key_insight: X Hedging replaces neural-network hedging policies with LightGBM tree ensembles, aiming to retain hedging performance while improving efficiency and explainability.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tree ensembles offer a practical alternative for dynamic option hedging when training data, compute resources, or model transparency are constraints.
method: Use LightGBM tree ensembles to estimate hedging strategies.
Train models sequentially within a reinforcement-learning-style hedging framework.
Introduce stochasticity through randomized training orders.
infographic.evidence_signal: Controlled experiments report performance comparable to Deep Hedging, improved computational efficiency, greater user-centered explainability, and substantially higher robustness with limited training data.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative metrics or evaluation details, leaving the size and generalizability of the reported gains unclear.
infographic.paper_title: X Hedging: towards an eXplainable artificial intelligence option Hedging framework

title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?
authors: Myeong-Su Lee
abstract: Adding constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the loss has been reported to improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in several applications, but mathematical understanding of these benefits remains limited. For several partial differential equations (PDEs), we derive stability estimates for losses with and without integral constraints. The comparison reveals that in certain parameter regimes, the standard loss has very weak control over specific error components, and that the integral constraints restore uniform control of these components. This explains when and why the constraints improve accuracy. Finally, numerical experiments support this interpretation. In parameter regimes where the standard loss is predicted to have weak control over those components, the two losses indeed show clear differences in accuracy. Conversely, in regimes where the standard loss retains sufficient control, both losses yield similar accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Integral constraints can improve PINN accuracy by restoring uniform control over error components that standard losses constrain only weakly in certain PDE parameter regimes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adding integral constraints is most useful when the governing PDE and its parameters leave important solution errors weakly controlled by the standard PINN loss.
method: Add constraints obtained by integrating governing equations to the PINN loss.
Derive and compare stability estimates with and without integral constraints for several PDEs.
Test predicted accuracy differences through numerical experiments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments show clear accuracy differences in regimes predicted to have weak standard-loss control, but similar accuracy when that control remains sufficient.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits are parameter-dependent; integral constraints should not be assumed to improve accuracy across all PDEs or regimes.
infographic.paper_title: When and why can integral constraints improve the accuracy of physics-informed neural networks?

title: Large-Scale Tensor Trace-Ratio Problem: Randomized Algorithm and Sparse Multilinear Discriminant Analysis via Closed-Form Solution
authors: Yuhang Li, Gang Wu
abstract: Trace-ratio optimization problems from high-dimensional tensor data appear across numerous research domains including machine learning, signal processing, as well as pattern recognition. Up to now, analytical closed-form expressions remain unavailable for tensor trace-ratio tasks; prevailing techniques mostly adopt inner-outer iterative schemes to tackle such optimization tasks. However, when dealing with high-dimensional tensor data sets, existing multilinear discriminant analysis methods often encounter limitations such as heavy computational costs, insufficient memory space, and interference from redundant features. This paper yields two core contributions.First, we present a closed-form solution under the full row rank condition, and construct a randomized solver targeting large-scale tensor trace-ratio optimization. In contrast to prior approaches, the devised algorithm achieves substantial computational speedup.Its core mechanism is to reformulate the original large-scale tensor trace-ratio optimization into a tensor least-squares formulation, instead of the much more complicated (generalized) tensor eigenproblems. We derive theoretical error-bound results which verify the reliability of the newly developed algorithm. Second, we build a sparse multilinear discriminant analysis model leveraging the above closed-form result combined with tensor \ell_{2,0}-norm regularization, and propose a sparse multilinear discriminant method for tensor feature selection. The sparse method can identify key discriminative features from high-dimensional data and suppress redundant information. Comprehensive numerical evaluations are conducted over multiple publicly available real-world benchmarks.The proposed methods demonstrate significant advantages in computational efficiency and scalability for large-scale problems, while achieving competitive classification accuracy on some datasets.

infographic.key_insight: Under a full row rank condition, tensor trace-ratio optimization admits a closed-form solution that enables a randomized large-scale solver and sparse discriminative feature selection.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets computational cost, memory constraints, and redundant features when learning from high-dimensional tensor data.
method: Reformulate tensor trace-ratio optimization as tensor least squares rather than tensor eigenproblems.
Construct a randomized solver with theoretical error bounds.
Combine the closed-form result with tensor ℓ₂,₀ regularization for sparse multilinear discriminant analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on multiple public real-world benchmarks report efficiency and scalability advantages, with competitive classification accuracy on some datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The closed-form guarantee requires full row rank; applicability should be checked for rank-deficient data.
infographic.paper_title: Large-Scale Tensor Trace-Ratio Problem: Randomized Algorithm and Sparse Multilinear Discriminant Analysis via Closed-Form Solution

title: Stochastic counterpart of Nesterov's method for sampling and provable non-acceleration of samplers with heavy-ball structure
authors: A. Sharma
abstract: Polyak's heavy-ball method and Nesterov's method are two momentum-based methods that have inspired many optimization techniques used in applied fields, including machine learning. Momentum also provides a connection with sampling, and interestingly, many kinetic Langevin samplers reduce to the heavy-ball recurrence when velocity is eliminated and noise is removed. This observation motivates a natural question: what is the corresponding sampler for Nesterov's method? We propose a sampler whose deterministic part is exactly Nesterov's recurrence, driven by temporally correlated Gaussian noise and requires one new gradient evaluation per step. Noise correlation provides $\mathcal{O}(h^2)$ bias for smooth observables. We establish geometric ergodicity for possibly non-convex potentials. For strongly convex potentials with Lipschitz continuous gradients, we obtain contraction rates and show that, up to an additive constant, the energy decays at a rate of order $κ^{-1/2}$, where $κ$ is the condition number. For Gaussian targets, we show that relaxation has square-root dependence on $κ$. We further prove that any sampler based on heavy-ball dynamics with additive noise cannot achieve accelerated convergence uniformly over the class of strongly convex functions. Finally, we compare the proposed sampler with OBABO, BAOAB, HMC, MALA, BPS, and NUTS in numerical experiments and demonstrate the better performance of proposed sampler.

infographic.key_insight: A sampler with Nesterov’s deterministic recurrence and correlated Gaussian noise achieves square-root condition-number scaling in stated settings, while additive-noise heavy-ball samplers cannot accelerate uniformly over strongly convex functions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method offers a momentum-based sampling approach for ill-conditioned distributions using one new gradient evaluation per step.
method: Combine Nesterov’s recurrence with temporally correlated Gaussian noise.
Establish geometric ergodicity for possibly non-convex potentials and O(h²) bias for smooth observables.
Analyze strongly convex contraction and Gaussian relaxation, and prove a heavy-ball non-acceleration result.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees and numerical comparisons showing better performance than OBABO, BAOAB, HMC, MALA, BPS, and NUTS, without specifying benchmarks or effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Square-root scaling is established under specific assumptions and should not be interpreted as uniform acceleration for general non-convex targets.
infographic.paper_title: Stochastic counterpart of Nesterov's method for sampling and provable non-acceleration of samplers with heavy-ball structure

title: Reinforcement Learning Unlearns Corrupted SFT Reasoning
authors: Anika Misra, Shreyas Vinod, Huteng Dai
abstract: We show that reinforcement learning (RL) in reasoning tasks can succeed even when the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) data is severely corrupted. In a mathematical reasoning dataset (GSM8K), we systematically corrupt training trajectories across 361 configurations by injecting realistic error types, varying error locations, trace-answer consistency, and corruption ratios up to 100%. While aggregated SFT-only performance steadily deteriorates under corruption (dropping from 43.61% to 13.80%), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training consistently restores model accuracy back to gold-baseline levels (approximately 60%). Crucially, initializing RL with as few as N = 8 minimal, incorrect, three-line "form-only" traces boosts post-RL performance to 69.30%, outperforming standard gold SFT initialization (60.71%) and GRPO without SFT (35.00%). Further, we show that SFT accuracy is largely uncorrelated with post-RL accuracy (r approximately 0), demonstrating a fundamental asymmetry in post-training: SFT primarily establishes structural layout (form), while RL independently discovers functional reasoning (function).

infographic.key_insight: On GSM8K, RL recovered accuracy after severely corrupted supervised fine-tuning, suggesting that SFT can supply reasoning format while RL learns effective reasoning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Minimal, even incorrect, format-setting traces may provide a useful RL initialization without requiring extensive gold reasoning demonstrations.
method: Tested 361 SFT corruption configurations varying error type, location, trace–answer consistency, and corruption ratio up to 100%.
Applied Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) after SFT and compared mathematical reasoning accuracy.
Evaluated initialization with just eight incorrect, three-line “form-only” traces.
infographic.evidence_signal: SFT-only accuracy fell from 43.61% to 13.80% under corruption, while GRPO generally restored roughly 60%; eight form-only traces yielded 69.30%, versus 60.71% with gold SFT and 35.00% without SFT.
infographic.watch_item: The reported evidence is from GSM8K; transfer to other tasks, model scales, and reward settings remains unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning Unlearns Corrupted SFT Reasoning

title: Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?
authors: Han Yan, Jin Zhu, Chengchun Shi, Tengyao Wang
abstract: Semiparametric models provide a broad framework for statistical inference, yet efficient estimation typically relies on influence function correction tailored to each estimand and on nuisance estimation repeated for every sample. We show that a single pretrained Transformer can deliver efficient estimation and valid inference for a family of estimands in one forward pass, without deriving efficient influence functions or estimating nuisance functions. Pretrained on simulated data with the true parameter as the only label, the Transformer learns the posterior mean and covariance of the queried estimand and hence returns an estimate and a Wald-type confidence region. Theoretically, we prove that, for locally flat pretraining priors of slowly growing complexity, the posterior mean is efficient for every queried estimand. The Transformer inherits this efficiency with asymptotically exact coverage, in probability over evaluation populations and queries, even under distribution shift. We also reveal that the guarantee places much higher demands on pretraining when the data-generating distribution is fixed, as in classical frequentist inference. Experiments on causal inference, partial linear regression, and survival analysis show that the pretrained model generally achieves the lowest estimation error among competing methods, with nearly nominal coverage, at a computational cost of only about 0.02 seconds per dataset.

infographic.key_insight: A single pretrained Transformer can deliver semiparametrically efficient estimates and asymptotically valid confidence regions for multiple queried estimands in one forward pass, under stated theoretical conditions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could replace repeated nuisance fitting and estimand-specific influence-function derivations with fast, reusable inference.
method: Pretrain on simulated datasets using true parameters as the only labels.
Predict each queried estimand’s posterior mean and covariance to construct a Wald-type confidence region.
Establish efficiency under locally flat pretraining priors of slowly growing complexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments in causal inference, partial linear regression, and survival analysis generally achieved the lowest estimation error among competing methods, nearly nominal coverage, and about 0.02 seconds per dataset.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees hold in probability over evaluation populations and queries, including under distribution shift, but fixed-population frequentist guarantees require substantially more demanding pretraining.
infographic.paper_title: Can pretrained Transformers deliver semiparametrically efficient inference?

title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers
authors: Wei Jiang, Ziran Liu, Wei Wang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) theorem solvers differ in both proving capability and inference cost. Applying an expensive solver to every subgoal wastes computation when cheaper models are sufficient, while always starting from the cheapest solver wastes attempts on subgoals that require stronger models. We present BudgetPV, an agentic budget-aware predict-and-verify system that allocates computation across unresolved subgoals and heterogeneous LLM solvers. BudgetPV uses a cross-solver predictor to guide solver selection for each subgoal and revises the allocation as verification feedback becomes available. The allocation problem changes as proving progresses. Early decisions mainly determine which solver should handle an untried subgoal, while later decisions determine which previously attempted subgoals should receive additional computation. We train the predictor with two objectives for these two stages. Class-weighted cross-entropy improves assignment to less frequent stronger solvers during the initial stage, while plain cross-entropy provides better calibrated probabilities for later allocation among previously attempted subgoals. We evaluate BudgetPV on Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench using three progressively expanded solver settings: a strong but expensive solver alone, adding a medium-cost solver with intermediate solving capability, and further adding a cheap solver with lower solving capability. BudgetPV requires less LLM generation computation than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals across the evaluated settings. The experiments further show the computation savings obtained as medium- and lower-cost solvers are added.

infographic.key_insight: BudgetPV reduces theorem-proving generation compute by predicting which solver each subgoal needs and updating allocations using verification feedback.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Routing subgoals across heterogeneous LLMs can reserve expensive inference for harder proofs rather than applying one solver uniformly.
method: Use a cross-solver predictor to select solvers for unresolved subgoals.
Revise computation allocations as verification feedback arrives.
Train with class-weighted cross-entropy for initial assignment and plain cross-entropy for later allocation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across Lean Workbook, miniF2F, ProofNet, and PutnamBench, BudgetPV uses less LLM generation compute than uniform allocation to solve the same number of subgoals in the evaluated solver settings.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify savings or establish whether they outweigh predictor and verification overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Budget-Aware Predict-and-Verify Theorem Proving with Heterogeneous LLM Solvers

title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models
authors: Mengxiao Gao, Elly K. H. Hung, Yuchen Wu, Yi Yu
abstract: Estimating the score function of a distribution plays a central role in statistics and machine learning, with applications in distribution estimation, sampling, and score-based generative modeling. However, learning scores from sensitive data raises privacy concerns. These concerns are particularly pronounced in score-based generative modeling, where trained models may memorize individual training examples and expose sensitive information through membership inference and data extraction attacks. Although non-private score estimation has been extensively studied, the statistical limits of its private counterpart remain less understood. In this work, we study score estimation under $(α,β)$-differential privacy for $d$-dimensional sub-Gaussian distributions with locally $γ$-Hölder-continuous scores. We develop a sampling-based private score estimator using quadratic B-splines and the exponential mechanism, and we implement our proposal through projected Langevin Monte Carlo with runtime polynomial in the sample size $n$. The proposed estimator satisfies $(α,β)$-differential privacy, and achieves expected density-weighted squared error $\mbox{polylog}(n) \max(n^{-2γ/(d+2γ+2)},\,(nα)^{-2γ/(d+γ+1)})$. We also establish a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, thereby characterizing the privacy-accuracy trade-off for score estimation. As an application, we construct a differentially private diffusion model whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps. We show that, with an appropriate discretization scheme, the resulting diffusion model attains nearly minimax optimal expected total variation error among all private distribution estimators. We validate our theoretical findings through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

infographic.key_insight: Private score estimation achieves a nearly minimax-optimal privacy–accuracy trade-off and enables diffusion models whose privacy guarantee is independent of the number of denoising steps.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a theoretically grounded route to privacy-preserving generative modeling, with an implementation whose runtime is polynomial in sample size.
method: Represent scores with quadratic B-splines and sample an estimator using the exponential mechanism.
Implement private estimation via projected Langevin Monte Carlo.
Use the private scores in a suitably discretized diffusion model.
infographic.evidence_signal: The paper establishes error upper bounds and a nearly matching private minimax lower bound, and reports experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees assume sub-Gaussian distributions with locally Hölder-continuous scores; polynomial runtime alone does not establish scalability in high dimensions.
infographic.paper_title: Differentially Private Score Estimation with Applications to Score-Based Generative Models

title: A 3D PINN-Based Framework for Patient-Specific Pulmonary Hemodynamics Using Windkessel Models
authors: Celia Taboada, Luis Nuñez, Angélica Casero, Pedro Navas
abstract: Cardiovascular fluid dynamics modeling relies heavily on mesh-based numerical methods such as Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). While accurate, these methods entail significant computational costs and complex meshing workflows that limit their translation to clinical practice. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a promising meshless alternative that embeds the governing equations directly into neural network training. In this work, we propose a PINN framework for pulsatile blood flow in patient-specific geometries with dynamic lumped-parameter Windkessel (RCR) outlet conditions representing distal vascular impedance. Coupling the Windkessel ODE to a 3D network raises two difficulties: the ODE alone does not fix the pressure level, and the local pressure variations that drive the flow are orders of magnitude smaller than the basal pressure imposed by the outlet. We address them by decomposing pressure into a time-dependent basal part and a spatially varying part, an initial condition and gauge for the Windkessel equation, a global mass-balance constraint, and a periodic Fourier embedding of time. Validated on 2D canonical channels (steady and pulsatile, with and without RCR outlet), the framework is then applied to a patient-specific right pulmonary artery, reproducing outlet flow, mean pressure, and the velocity and dynamic pressure fields with errors on the order of the data resolution. Finally, we solve the inverse problem of identifying the three Windkessel parameters of the outlet from synthetic data, recovering them with errors of about 0.3% from deliberately wrong initial values. Residual biases in the local pressure field and the need to test robustness to noisy clinical data remain open, but the results support PINNs as complementary tools for meshless hemodynamics and patient-specific digital twins.

infographic.key_insight: A 3D physics-informed neural network couples patient-specific pulmonary blood flow with Windkessel outlet models by separating basal pressure from small spatial pressure variations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a meshless complement to CFD for patient-specific hemodynamics and estimation of distal vascular parameters.
method: Embed blood-flow equations and dynamic Windkessel RCR outlet conditions in PINN training.
Separate basal and spatial pressure, with a Windkessel initial condition, pressure gauge, and global mass-balance constraint.
Use periodic Fourier time embedding to represent pulsatile flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on 2D channels and a patient-specific right pulmonary artery reproduced flow and pressure at errors on the order of data resolution; inverse estimation recovered three Windkessel parameters from synthetic data with about 0.3% error.
infographic.watch_item: Residual local-pressure biases remain, and robustness to noisy clinical data has not yet been established.
infographic.paper_title: A 3D PINN-Based Framework for Patient-Specific Pulmonary Hemodynamics Using Windkessel Models

title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning
authors: Zeguan Xiao, Zhuocheng Liang, Yun Chen, Yong Wang, Guanhua Chen, Pinyan Lu
abstract: A central challenge in adapting large language models (LLMs) is capability preservation: an adaptation can achieve its target while degrading general capabilities. We introduce CurvDelta, a scalable framework that incorporates the preservation constraint into the parameterization of the model update. By analyzing the local geometry of the preservation constraint around the pre-adaptation model, CurvDelta constructs a low-curvature space in which parameter updates leave the preservation loss nearly invariant. We make its construction practical for LLMs through Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and a factorized projection. We also introduce CurvLoRA, a low-rank variant within the same preservation geometry, designed for more efficient adaptation. Both methods apply to preservation-constrained adaptation tasks such as capability learning and selective unlearning. We evaluate our methods on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and knowledge unlearning. For mathematical reasoning and code generation, our approaches achieve competitive downstream performance while better preserving general capabilities, offering a favorable acquisition--retention trade-off relative to the baselines. For knowledge unlearning, our main results on TOFU and MUSE show a better balance between targeted forgetting and knowledge retention than the baselines, with retention performance close to the from-scratch retraining reference.

infographic.key_insight: CurvDelta steers model updates into low-curvature directions of the preservation loss, enabling targeted learning or unlearning while limiting degradation of existing capabilities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a geometry-aware way to adapt LLMs when acquiring or removing specific capabilities must not compromise general performance.
method: Construct a low-curvature update space from the local geometry of the preservation loss around the original model.
Use Kronecker-factored approximate curvature (K-FAC) and factorized projection to make the construction scalable.
Apply CurvLoRA for low-rank adaptation within the same preservation geometry.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations cover mathematical reasoning, code generation, and TOFU/MUSE knowledge unlearning, reporting improved acquisition–retention or forgetting–retention trade-offs, with unlearning retention close to from-scratch retraining.
infographic.watch_item: Preservation relies on local, approximate curvature estimates; the abstract does not quantify computational overhead or robustness for large updates.
infographic.paper_title: CurvDelta: Low-Curvature Delta Modeling For Surgical Learning and Unlearning

title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI
authors: Oliver Schön, Adrien Banse, John Lygeros, Lars Lindemann
abstract: Robots can be controlled to perform tasks with guaranteed correctness when the task instructions are stated in a formal language. Large language models (LLMs) have been widely used to allow users to provide such instructions in natural language (NL), by translating NL into formal language. When deploying such translators on a robot, however, we face limited computing and energy resources, while offloading computation or data to the cloud may be infeasible or undesirable. Yet an LLM is a general-purpose text generator, whereas a formula in a fixed formal language fragment follows a well-defined syntax. We therefore ask whether text generation is needed at all. For the formal language of linear temporal logic (LTL), we show that this translation can instead be broken down into answering a set of questions with pre-defined answers. We then construct a System-One model, a recent class of NL-based classifier, to provide such answers and enable us to translate a natural language instruction into an LTL instruction. On three benchmarks, our translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs available, at up to one order of magnitude lower runtime and energy consumption. We show that it generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.

infographic.key_insight: Natural-language instructions can be translated into linear temporal logic (LTL) by answering predefined questions instead of generating text.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach supports on-device robot task translation with lower runtime and energy use, reducing reliance on cloud computation.
method: Decompose translation within a fixed LTL fragment into questions with predefined answers.
Use a System-One natural-language classifier to answer those questions.
Construct the LTL instruction from the predicted answers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three benchmarks, the translator matches or exceeds the accuracy of the best local LLMs evaluated, with up to an order-of-magnitude reduction in runtime and energy consumption, and generalizes to unseen atomic propositions and temporal patterns.
infographic.watch_item: Deployment should validate coverage of the supported LTL fragment and translation errors; formal task specifications alone do not guarantee that natural-language intent was captured correctly.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Natural Language to Temporal Logic Translation for Real-Time Physical AI

title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks
authors: Leevan Ling, Shu Ma, Yizhong Sun
abstract: Residual-based methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks, and some physics-informed neural operator architectures, approximate PDE solutions by minimizing a discrete least-squares loss formed from the PDE and boundary residuals over a prescribed trial class. This structure is shared by classical least-squares Kansa collocation, whose kernel trial spaces admit an established convergence theory. For neural trial classes, approximation power alone does not ensure that discrete residuals control the continuous solution error. For linear elliptic Dirichlet problems, we extend the kernel-based collocation framework to neural trial classes through elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency. Elliptic regularity supplies the PDE estimate relating solution error to continuous residuals. Discrete stability identifies admissible trial subclasses in which continuous residuals are controlled by a computable discrete loss. This step also quantifies the required number of collocation points. Furthermore, the stability analysis naturally demands a scale-dependent, physics-balanced boundary weight. For the constrained problem, consistency requires accurate comparison functions within the same admissible subclass, a requirement not supplied by neural approximation estimates alone. Specializing to multilayer perceptrons with tanh activations (tanh-MLPs), we construct admissible comparison networks and establish convergence for the constrained residual minimization problem. We further obtain conditional convergence of unconstrained physics-balanced PINNs based on tanh-MLPs under joint network and sampling refinement.

infographic.key_insight: Neural approximation power alone does not ensure PINN convergence; discrete stability and accurate comparison networks within admissible trial classes are also needed.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For linear elliptic Dirichlet PDEs, the framework guides collocation density and scale-dependent boundary weighting so discrete residual losses can control solution error.
method: Extend kernel collocation theory using elliptic regularity, discrete stability, and consistency.
Identify stable admissible neural subclasses and quantify collocation requirements with physics-balanced boundary weights.
Construct admissible tanh-MLP comparison networks to prove constrained convergence and conditional unconstrained convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence results for tanh-MLPs, not numerical benchmarks or empirical performance measurements.
infographic.watch_item: Unconstrained PINN convergence remains conditional under joint network and sampling refinement; approximation estimates alone do not establish the required stability and consistency.
infographic.paper_title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks
